maintopic: HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
HON. MR. MURDOCK AND HOME BANK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave
to present the second report of the select standing committee on Privileges and Elections. I also lay on the Table the evidence taken and the exhibits filed before said committee. The report is as follows:
Your committee, having considered the resolution referred to the select standing committee on Privileges and Elections on May 22, 1924, as follows:-
" Thursday, May, 22, 1924. Ordered,-That the following:-
Mr. Porter, seconded by Mr. Guthrie, moved, Tha/t, E. Guss Porter, member representing the electoral riding of West Hastings, in this House, having declared from his seat in the House that he is credibly informed and that he believes he is able to establish by satisfactory evidence that:-
The Honourable James Murdock, Minister of Labour, did withdraw from the Home Bank at its Ottawa branch on the 15th day of August, 1923, two days before such bank's failure, thousands of dollars on deposit therein to his credit, using certain information he had received, as such minister, of the likely immediate failure of said bank, and had received advantage and profit to himself to the extent of such withdrawals, contrary to his obligations as such minister in derogation of his office and the honour, dignity and traditions of parliament, be referred to the select standing committee on Privileges of this House to inquire fully into the said allegations with power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath or affirmation, and that the said committee do report in full the evidence taken before (them and all other procedure on the reference, and the result of their inquiries to this House for such action thereon as this House may determine.
Attest.
W. B. Northrup,
Clerk of the House of Commons." and having heard the evidence given by all witnesses submitted in support of the charge contained in said 
resolution and all evidence and statements made in answer thereto, and examined all exhibits filed on such inquiry, beg leave to report as follows:-
The evidence taken by the committee shows that Honourable James Murdock on the 15th of August, 1923, drew out of the Home Bank of Canada, at its Ottawa branch, the sum of $4,050, but there is no evidence to show that before so drawing out said sum he had received information as a cabinet minister, of the probable failure of said bank. The evidence also shows that the only information Mr. Murdock had of the probable failure of said bank was received as a private citizen from Honourable G. N. Gordon, in a friendly interview on the 9th of August, 1923.
The committee finds that Honourable James Murdock did nothing in connection with the withdrawal of such money from the Home Bank contrary to his obligation as a minister of the Crown, or in derogation of his office and the honour, dignity, and traditions of parliament, and that the charge submitted to this committee for investigation, so far as it affects the honour of Mr. Murdock, is not only not proved but entirely disproved.
Your committee submit herewith the minutes of proceedings and exhibits laid before the committee, and evidence taken by them.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
J. Archambault,
Chairman.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
North Toronto (Mr. Church) has handed me the following:
I ask leave to move an adjournment of the House under Rule 39 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely:
The application or request of the postal employees received by the government since yesterday for an amendment to the present statute relating to the revised schedule of wages by the Civil Service Commission and the refusal of the employees to accept the said schedule, and their intimation that within forty-eight hours a strike will occur which will, if allowed, cause great damage to trade and commerce and inconvenience to the public and to the business of parliament as well. And for the object of asking this hon. House to consider some form of conciliation, either by granting the employees a board of conciliation or otherwise, or by appointing a Select Committee of the House to consider the case and suggest amending legislation, if any, they deem just and advisable in the matter or for the purpose of taking such other or further action as is deemed advisable, and if leave is granted, I beg leave to move, seconded by Mr. Maclean (South York):	"That this House
do now adjourn."
Rule 39 reads:
(1)	A motion to adjourn (except when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) shall always be in order, but no second motion to the same effect shall be made until after some intermediate proceeding has been had.
(2)	Leave to make a motion for the adjournment of the House (when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance) must be asked after the ordinary daily routine of business (Rule 25) has been concluded and before notices of motions or orders of the day are entered upon.
The rule is that the Speaker must decide if the matter of the motion is of urgent public ' importance. The hon. member who makes the motion hands the Speaker a written statement of the matter, which the Speaker reads to the House. This I have done. The Speaker then asks whether the member has the leave of the House to make the motion. In my humble opinion this matter, a threatened strike which may paralyze the whole of the postal service in Canada, is a matter of urgent public importance. But there is another obligation which must follow my decision that it is a matter of urgent public importance, it is that if objection is taken more than twenty members must rise to indicate the desire that the member may proceed with his motion. So, if it is the desire of the House that the hon. member shall proceed, more than twenty members must rise.
The Clerk Assistant having stated that more than twenty members had risen.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I I have no intention of taking up more than three minutes of the time of the House on this occasion. The matter is a very important one to the entire city I represent. The members of the House have had no opportunity of discussing this question as they have been waiting for the estimates of the Postmaster General before dealing with the matter, and they have not even yet been considered. Neither have the civil service estimates been considered nor have we had an opportunity of discussing this matter and bringing the facts before the House.
The city from which I come contributes six million dollars to the postal revenue, and the business men of that city are becoming alarmed as to what may happen if some action is not taken by the government. This question has been hanging fire for several months past and tossed about to and fro. Some time ago the matter was considered, and the government assigned to the Civil Service Commission and the deputy ministers the duty of making a survey and drawing up a new schedule of salaries. The Prime Minister laid on the table the correspondence between the various boards considering the case and said it was not within the province of the government to take any action.
This matter was referred to the Audit Board and the Civil Service Commission, who have now made their report. It was bandied about from pillar to post, and the employees have become very much annoyed over the delay and the way in which the case has been handled. Notwithstanding the high cost of living to-day, the scale as recommended by the Civil Service Commission, turning the bonus into salary, works out at a reduction of $179,000 a year. I am not going to enter into any discussion o* the report of the Audit Board and the Civil Service Commission to the government, but the government might have taken the House into their confidence a little more and told the Civil Service Commission candidly: We are prepared to go so far in the revision of salaries upward. That has not been done.
The Civil Service Commission have been blamed by the government, and while I am
Postal Employees

not prepared to go so far as to say that they should be 'blamed or are at all to blame, I think the government and this House should do something to protect the country from the great inconvenience that will be caused if a strike occurs. The ultimatum I believe has been issued' and will expire in a few hours and if a strike happens it will paralyze business. Coming from an industrial city, I know how strikes tie up business. The business men of the country surely deserve some consideration, and a showdown on this whole question is requested. I know that the postal employees in the district from which I come are not the kickers; they are patriotic citizens and the last thing they would want to do is to inconvenience the public one iota. In view of that they have been long suffering and patient, and I hope the government has some favourable statement to make to-day in the matter. For these reasons I did not like to move this resolution, but many business men, commercial firms and public bodies in the city from which I come, requested me to bring the matter before the House and get some action on it. I could not get it before the House on the Orders of the Day nor on the Post Office estimates, and the only course I had open to me was to move this resolution. I have received numerous letters and telegrams from public bodies-a strike vote will be counted to-day at six o'clock; I have been told that the men are to strike.
It has taken nearly six years since the war ended for this bonus to be turned into a straight salary recommendation. The city of Toronto and outside commissions have about 12,000 employees to whom they used to give a war bonus; but as soon as they could after the war they turned the bonus into a straight salary. I urge upon the government to do something to avert this coming strike. What I suggest is that the employees are entitled to either, first, a board of conciliation under the Industrial Disputes Act or, second, a select committee of the House should be appointed to bring in a report within ten days recommending how far we should go in the matter of revision of the statute. If the House does something, a strike will be averted, but if a strike is not averted the trade and commerce of the country will be very seriously hampered. The facts are known to every one and I ask for immediate action before it is too late.

The application or request of the postal employees received by the government since yesterday for an amendment to the present statute relating to the revised schedule of wages by the Civil Service Commission and the refusal of the employees to accept the said schedule, and their intimation that within forty-eight hours a strike will occur which will, if allowed, cause great damage to trade and commerce and inconvenience to the public and to business of parliament as well.
That declaration, so far as the government is a-ware, is quite inaccurate. No application or request of the postal employees has been received by the government since yesterday. I do not know where my hon. friend got his information; but neither the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Stewart) nor myself- and I think it would be the one or the other to whom a communication of this kind would be addressed-has, up to the present time, received any such application as is referred to in the motion of my hon. friend. The motion uses the words,
their intimation that within forty-eight hours a strike will occur.
The government has received no intimation to that effect. Perhaps my hon. friend would tell the House the source of his information. I think it ought to be made perfectly clear to hon. members that since the schedule attached to the report of the Civil Service Commission has been sent to representatives of the postal employees, the government has received from them no official communication whatever. What has appeared in the press has appeared in the press without the knowledge of the government as to the sources from which the different declarations were emanating. Up to the present time no communication of the nature described in the motion has been received. On the other hand', I understand that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) and the Acting Post-

master General have both taken steps to intimate to representatives of the postal employees that they would be pleased to receive them in conference and hoped that any such action as that which was being referred to in the press would not be taken by them without the most careful consideration in every particular.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps my
hon. friend will let me proceed further with what I intend to say. When the government referred to the Civil Service Commission the revision of salaries of postal employees, that was part of a larger reference embracing the entire public service. The clause in the order in council in that connection reads:
The committee of the Privy Council, on the recommendation of the President of the Privy Council, advise that, in accordance with the announcement made by him in the House of Commons on the 19th March, 1924, (copy of which is submitted), the Civil Service Commission be directed to undertake immediately a revision of the salaries of the Civil Service of Canada and to report thereon to His Excellency in Council at as early a date as may be possible.
It is the salaries of the entire Civil Service of Canada that the Civil Service Commission is being asked to report upon at the present time. To oblige the postal employees, the government asked that their department be the first to be taken up by the Civil Service Commission, but that as soon as it was concluded, the other departments of the government should then be proceeded with. In the report which the Civil Service Commission made to the government on the 8th May, the following paragraph is included:
The importance of this revision in the postal service will be apparent when it is considered that increases in basic rates of compensation and consequent increased cost of the service would not be confined to the postal service, but must necessarily be also applied to the whole public service as the work of salary revision is proceeded with.
I hope that hon. members and1 the country will appreciate the significance of that statement in the report of the Civil Service Commission to the government,- that in taking up the revision of the salaries of postal employees they have had in mind the principles which will obtain with respect to the entire public service of the Dominion. The government feel that to take any action at this moment beyond approving what the Civil Service Commission has recommended might be most prejudicial to the further inquiry which the Civil Service Commission is making, inasmuch as the country will not know until the commission has concluded its examination of the revision what the cost to the country, of the practical application of the recommendations is going to be. We therefore feel that until we have before us the report from the Civil Service Commission with respect to the entire Civil Service we shall not be in a position to consider, as we should be able to consider in all its aspects, what the consequence would be of recommending to parliament any concession or any addition to the salaries of any classes of employees beyond what may be recommended by the Civil Service Commission.
We are prepared, when the Civil Service Commission has submitted its report upon the salaries of the entire Civil Service, to consider that report carefully in the light of all the material which we have before us and to make to parliament, if we think it advisable so to do, recommendations supplementing those which are contained in the report of the Civil Service Commission. But we do not feel that we are in a position to make any recommendations to parliament at the present time with respect to the postal employees; and I hope that the employees of the Post Office Department will see that the position which the government is taking is one which is in the interests of the entire Civil Service and in the interest of the taxpayers of the country as well.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
It does not seem fair that the
amounts to be paid to postal workers should be dependent upon the schedule as it may appertain to Civil Service workers generally. We are faced with a concrete situation at the present time; the postal workers claim very distinctly that the amount they receive is not sufficient to maintain a decent standard of living, and that fact will not be altered by any further considerations which the commission may bring forward. I would- submit that throughout the country generally there is a very considerable interest in this matter and there is a strong sentiment in favour of an increase in the salaries of postal workers. When this matter was being discussed some months ago I noticed an article in the Toronto Telegram

not one of the most radical of Canadian journals-under date April 19, which summarized somewhat as follows:
The jab-a postal porter's helper.
The hours-4.30 a.m, to 12 p.m., six days a week.
The work-handling filled mail bags 50 to 100 pounds.
The pay-$8.50 a week.
That probably represents the lowest grade of the service. On the other hand the great majority of the postal workers are engaged

in very responsible work and they receive in many instances less than is supposed, according to the statistics furnished by our own departments, to be the minimum cost of living. Permit me to read a paragraph or two from a recent issue of the Winnipeg Evening Tribune.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I desire now to
quote a paragraph or two from the Winnipeg Evening Tribune of Wednesday, the 11th instant:
The new scale, by abolishing the bonus and substituting a 15 per cent increase of the basic salaries, will, it is true, raise the pay of some of the higher officials over what was. proposed last March. But for married men in the medium grades the salaries will in many classes be even further reduced.
Letter carriers in the top grade, for instance, were paid during the last fiscal year at the rate of 11,557 per annum. This amount included $1,260 salary and $297 bonus. In March last it was proposed to cut the bonus by $99 so that the total maximum salary and bonus would equal $1,458. The letter carriers protested to the government against this reduction, and quoted official figures to show that the reduced salary was well below the level set by the Dominion Department of Labour for a decent standard of living for a family of five persons.
There was some unfortunate talk of a strike, but the government poured oil on the troubled waters by promising reconsideration of the salary schedule. It is now proposed as a brilliant solution of the problem that the bonus shall be dropped altogether and that the basic salaries shall be raised about 15 per cent. The letter carriers are thus offered a maximum of $1,440 a year, which is $117 less than t-hey received last year and $18 less than the protested schedule of last March .... It is not too late for the blunder to be rectified. It is understood the Prime Minister has yet to confer with the postal employees. The people of Canada do not begrudge a fair wage to their public servants in exchange for faithful and honest service, and few fair-minded people will consider $1,440 a year to be adequate remuneration for a letter carrier of experience and integrity who faithfully performs his arduous duties.
It is not my intention to go into any comparison of the new. with the old schedules. From a number of our western cities we have received telegrams urging that there should be a revision of the proposed rates. I think that the general opinion is that the range should be from $1,260 to $1,980. Now, Mr. Speaker, the question is, what can be done in the face of the present serious situation? It is several months since the protests were made, and the postal employees have done

Postal Employees
apparently all in their power by what are termed constitutional means; that is to say, they have preferred their requests to the government and made their representations to the Civil Service Commission. The postal employees have protested also through members of parliament. What more can be done, so far as they are concerned? They seem to be driven to take direct action. Unfortunately there are members of the business community who are willing to push the matter to the limit. I read one sentence from a bulletin published by the Employers' Association of Manitoba, in which the solicitor of the association submits the following:
In ray judgment action should be taken immediately by the business interests to anticipate and prevent any interruption of the postal service. A strike by postal employees is essentially of a revolutionary character and ought not to be tolerated. There should be a law forbidding strikes by government employees and others engaged in operating public utilities.
Now, if there is no means of redress by an appeal to parliament what other course can the postal workers take than to refuse to continue working under conditions which do not assure them a decent living? That seems to me to be the situation with which we are faced at the present time. But' the postal workers are told that since they are operating a public utility a strike by them would be regarded as revolutionary in character! I quite admit that the postal employees do occupy a peculiar position. I think they feel their responsibility and realize that they ought not to strike unless it is absolutely imperative. But what other course remains open to them? You cannot reduce them to a condition of slavery. If they are urged not to strike, surely we in this House ought to be able to offer them some alternative. We ask the Prime Minister what can be done, and he says, "We are in the hands of the Civil Service Commission; we cannot do anything without altering the Civil Service Act."

speechtext:
If that is the case,
if we must take no action until that report is received, I would submit that in the meantime we should continue the present scale of wages with bonus, as my colleague (Mr. Irvine) has suggested.
I would urge upon the House the serious situation in which many of these postal workers find themselves. They are working on a very narrow margin; ten, twenty, fifty dollars may not mean a great deal to the majority of hon. members, but the smallest of these amounts means a very great deal to the rank and file of the postal employees; and if they were assured that, without prejudice, their case would receive full consideration, I am inclined to think that they might agree to the final settlement being deferred. But the matter has gone on month after month, in fact almost year after year-for the bonus has been regarded as a temporary provision- and consequently there has been a feeling of unrest and dissatisfaction in the service for several years while the final settlement was pending. Then when at last the settlement proves to be of this nature, it leaves them absolutely in despair of receiving? what they regard as justice. I would urge that these civil servants, who have been doing faithful work for many years, have a right to look to parliament for some redress, and that at this time the government ought to assume definite responsibilities and not plunge the country into the throes of a general strike.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was rather surprised to hear from the Prime Minister that he had received no intimation whatever from the postal employees, for the newspapers generally have recorded meetings of the various branches of the Postal Workers' Association throughout the country, at which meetings the men decided in favour of a strike unless their position was altered. I think it would be humiliating for the government if the difficulty ended in a strike and the business of the country was thrown into confusion, as in that event appeals for a prompt settlement would come from all over the Dominion, and the government would have to act. I would respectfully urge that the suggestion made, I think first by the member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine), and subsequently repeated by the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Woodsworth), that the full bonus of last year be continued, be acted on by the government, pending a final settlement. I do not think the postal workers have ever been unreasonable in theiir demands, and they have always put them forward in a reasonable manner. I think if this concession were granted it would avert the threatened strike. But if the matter is allowed to drift until it culminates in a strike, at will be more

Postal Employees

difficult to settle the trouble then than by anticipating it now and making the concession which has been suggested.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to associate myself with the remarks of my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Raymond). On several occasions already in this House I have discussed at some length the bonus as applied to the cost of living, and it seems to me that in this case the bonus granted last year, which even then was a reduction of the bonus for the preceding year, should remain until a settlement is effected not only of the remuneration of the postal workers but of that of all other branches of the Civil Service. Pending the full report on civil service salary revision, it would seem to me that we should not do anything to lower the already low rates which we pay our public sendee. This House would then have a chance to determine what is fair and right. Therefore I should be very pleased if the government could arrange to continue the cost of living bonus granted last year. I have yet to see any fall in the cost of living figures, and certainly until there has been a decided decline it is only fair and right that this concession should be made. By so doing we are not taking anything away from the postal workers or any other members of the Civil Service until the question is finally decided by an appeal to parliament, if necessary.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find myself in full aocord with the proposal to continue the cost of living bonus until a final adjustment is made. If we wait until the final report on salary revision is brought down before taking action, this session of parliament will probably close, and the civil service employees will be in a state of uncertainty and the country will suffer. I can truthfully say that in the western cities at least the cost of living has not gone down to such a point as to enable a family to be maintained on less than $100 a month, which represents the income of some of these men. I think the trouble with this country is that the big salaries are too big and the small salaries are too small. Some adjustment should be made, and I think the government should take this into consideration and act at once so as to satisfy those who are getting these lower salaries.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we had a postal strike in this country a few years ago, and the business of everybody in the country was so seriously hampered that it was found almost impossible to carry on. That manifestly must be the case in
TMr. Raymond.]
the event of any strike in the postal service. The only thing which, to my mind, would be worse than a postal strike would be a strike of railway emplojmes. There are some things about the adjustment that perhaps do not meet' with the view expressed by the officials of the department. But we have to bear in mind that the Civil Service Commission have facilities for getting information with respect to the cost' of living, and if hon. gentlemen will refer to the order in council they will find that due consideration was to be given by them to the cost of living and the payment' of salaries in occupations similar to those of the postal employees. The report of the Civil Service Commission states that they have done that; they have inquired carefully into the cost of living. That is what1 they say in their report; I am not speaking from my own knowledge because I have not got information on this question. * Not only that but the deputy ministers of the departments were associated with them in discussing this matter. Afterwards the whole case was reviewed by the Audit Board who had all this information placed before them. Hon. gentlemen now have in their possession the schedule which was the result of ail this investigation.
I am not going to take time to go into the whole matter this afternoon. I simply wish to say to hon. gentlemen-whether they are in favour of the Civil Service Commission or are opposed to them-that I think we can agree they are an impartial body to deal with a matter of this kind. Now, the postal employees, to be fair to them, complained they were not given full opportunity to present their case. I asked that the Civil Service Commission hear the postal employees; and a second time they complained that they were uf't, given sufficient time to place their case before the commission. Furthermore the postal employees had an interview with the Audit Board and, I understand, they discussed their case very fully with that body. As a

At the conclusion of the war, when our soldiers were coming home and it was difficult for them to get employment, the age limit was abandoned and married men became eligible for employment. Consequently in their case the salaries were found

Postal Employees
50 be too low. In considering this matter also it must be borne in mind that there are certain perquisites in the way of clothing that go with the salary and are still continued. I am not dwelling unduly upon that, but I want to say this: The result of the investigation is almost unanimous with respect to the salaries for those in the lower grades, but there is a difference of $60 between the recommendation of the Audit Board and that of the Civil Service Commission, and an even greater difference between the amount suggested by the officials of the department and the salary asked for by the employees. I am speaking now of the maximum salary, although the same remark applies to both the minimum and the maximum salaries. The point I want to emphasize is that throughout this investigation all agreed, or practically agreed, upon the minimum salary, and so recommended to the government. We have had that recommendation before us and it was returned to the Civil Service Commission upon two occasions. Hon. gentlemen have the memorandum of the commission before them and I am not going to refer to it, but the commission explain how they arrive at their conclusions. The statement of the government now is that when salaries generally are revised they are prepared to act on that basis and make it effective to the whole service. We have had that statement from the Prime Minister to-day and I am not going to dwell upon it.
My hon. friend (Mr. Church) makes a statement that the government have been notified officially by the officers of the Postal Employees organization that we had twenty-four hours in which to come to a satisfactory agreement with them. Well, we have no knowledge officially of that statement. It appears in the press but the department has received no information to that effect, and the Prime Minister has not been officially informed with respect to it. I did expect that when the postal employees-because we were constantly in touch with them; Mr. Murdock and I met them upon every occasion they came to Ottawa-had time to examine the schedule and had discussed it with their fellow employees we would probably have a further conference with them. I do not know whether they propose to adhere to the schedule they originally filed, or whether they would be willing to accept a modified one. If they adhere to that schedule its adoption would mean an additional expenditure in the Post Office Department of over $2,000,000. I am not saying that if that sum is required to give these employees a decent living it should not be granted, but I think the matter would want some further consideration than even the government or the House are prepared to accord it at this moment. I do not in any way suggest that we are shutting the door in the face of these employees, and are going to deny to them the right to discuss this matter with us and thresh it out until we reach a decision that will be satisfactory and avoid further difficulty. Nobody wants a strike. I would be the last to deny to the worker the right to take whatever action he sees fit and proper in order to protect his own interest. But surely civil servants, employees of the government and of parliament, are in a vastly different position to that occupied by the different workers throughout the country.
Do not assume that I am denying them the right of negotiation, the right of protest, or the right to take every proper means to bring legitimate grievances to the attention of the government or to those who may be in authority; but I do most solemnly protest and object to them taking such drastic action as would tie up the business of the country by way of strike. I think in fairness to the House and to myself I should make my position very plain. I have stated to the employees themselves that, so far as I am concerned, I am prepared in every legitimate way to give the postal employees or any other employees of this government what they are entitled to. But what does a strike mean? What will be the result of the strike? If one would judge by the temper of some of the speakers this afternoon, it means that parliament must succumb to the rights of the postal employees, without consideration of the question whether it is right or wrong, in order to avoid trouble. Surely the parliament of Canada is going to reserve to itself the right to run this country. Surely we cannot surrender that right, no matter what we may think about it, and I for one am prepared to go the limit. I am prepared to discuss with these men to-night, to-morrow or at any time, their legitimate grievances, and to sit down with them at any time and go into the matter. I have not the authority at the moment to say what the salaries shall be. In fairness to the Civil Service Commission, I say that they have gone into this matter conscientiously and fairly and made their finding. Perhaps further material might be brought to their attention, but if so I do not know of it at the moment. As far as I am able, I am prepared on all occasions to give to the civil servants of the country a fair deal; but I would deplore drastic action in the way of a

strike, and I think every hon. gentleman in this House would agree with me in that connection. It should be a very last recourse in industrial concerns; but so far as the police forces and the civil servants of the country are concerned, I cannot agree that it is warranted under any circumstances.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
That is the question that I have put to myself since the system of bonuses was commenced in the public service. If the civil service employees are not satisfied with their jobs, why do they not give them up and go to work on the farms? They will find out pretty soon that if they could get back their jobs they would take them as quickly as possible. In Ottawa what do we see on the streets every morning? People running, not working, but running because they are late, sometimes, for nine o'clock. If the people were to do that in the country, it would be pretty late in the morning before the cows were milked. The job is not the same at all.
As regards the situation in Montreal and other big cities, the claim is made that the postal employees want to go on strike. If people were wanted to fill their places, I think I could send to Montreal the next morning about 1,000 people who would be willing to give up their jobs at the brick yard at La-prairie or Delson and be pleased to go to Montreal, take those jobs and work five or six hours a day.
I do not object to a poor man with a family receiving a fair salary. The lowest, as stated by the minister, is $1,020. Where is the man in the country, where is the man at the brickyard at Laprairie, who makes as much as that? Our people get only $3 a day and they work about seven or eight months a year. They are, however, getting along all right. They raise families; their children are well clad and have shoes to go to school with, although their father has a salary of less than $1,000 a year. The trouble with the people in the cities is that they spend a little too much money to go to the movies sometimes; they go to bed too late and they acquire some habits, smoking cigarettes and that sort of thing on which they spend money for nothing. We, the farmers and the workingmen of the brickyards of Laprairie and Delson do not acquire those bad habits. We put that money in a sure place, that is, into the hands of the good woman who keeps the house and saves the money 'for us. We cannot go to the movies or smoke good cigars or good cigarettes. We buy meat, bread and sometimes molasses, and that is all we want. So I have been all my lifetime a man who has taken good care of money, and I think that is the only way to make a little money even though it takes a long time. That would not have been the case had I been a man to spend money for all the opportunities that come before me, for things that are pleasant enough sometimes. It is very pleasant to smoke a good cigar costing twenty or twenty-five cents, but I smoke that just on Sunday; and if I

had any advice to give to the civil service employees, it would be for them to follow my footsteps. In that way, I believe in the long run they would not find it necessary to come before the Civil Service Commission or before parliament, and they would likely be able to save money. I understand that we want to be able in the near future to make both ends meet; that this parliament is not yet too well off, and when a man in private life is not too well off, he cannot spend money for nothing. I should like to see economy practised, and the government should set the example for the rest of the community. When my right hon. friend was in opposition, I discussed the question of bonuses for civil service employees. What I said then, I say the same thing now. I trust the government will find a way of having fewer employees, paying them better and endeavouring to get from the same employees a good day's work. That is all I want.

I agree with the sentiments of the
hon. member (Mr. Lanctot) who has just concluded as well as with the remarks of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys). 1 understand that some hon. gentlemen are of the opinion that remarks of the nature I am going to make are out of order, but I shall try not to depart from the rules in the few minutes I shall occupy. In the matter under discussion to-day we are faced with one of the real problems which this parliament will have to deal with sooner or later. The wage problem in this country is a serious one, and it is all the more serious at the present time because it has got out of balance. One section of our public service is now insisting that it shall retain the pay which it received during the time of the high cost of living. The fact of the matter is that we still have a high cost of living; the cost of living has not gone down, and the question naturally is, what is the reason for this? Well, the cost of living is high, for one thing because wages are high; and how we are going to reduce that cost of living is the important question. As the hon. member for South Simcoe observed, letter carriers who are receiving to-day $600 for travelling twenty miles daily during twelve months of the year must subscribe to the cost of maintaining the city employees with whom we are dealing to-day; he has to give the other man twice as much as he himself is getting. It may be said that the cost of living is higher in the city than it is in the country; but as a matter of fact the man who has to keep two horses and a rig in the country on $600 has a harder problem to

Postal Employees
cope with than the city employee getting SI,200. I have no hesitation in saying that in my opinion every man engaged in a useful and honest occupation ought to be given such wages as will keep his family respectably and comfortably, afford his children an education, and allow him to put 'by something for a rainy day. If a worker is not able to do that because his wages will not permit it, then I say his wages are not high enough.
Now, there are two ways in which we can help the workers to realize this condition; we can either increase wages or bring down the cost of living. In my opinion it is imperative that the cost of living shall be reduced, because as I have said on two or three occasions one half of the people receive half of the wages which the other half of the wage-earners are given for their work. That state of things cannot continue, and as the last speaker remarked, there is no better way in which parliament can approach this subject than by reducing the indemnities of its own members. I have said that before.
I know that some members of parliament might perhaps be justified in going on strike if that were done, as they might not be getting enough compensation for their time. But we all know how we are spending our indemnity; there is no denying it. I think we could do with less if we saw fit. So far as the present question is concerned, as has been observed, unless we are prepared to treat alike all the employees in the various departments we can do nothing at present; there should be no discrimination. When we can put every man in the employment of the government on an even basis it will be quite right to make a change. But in the meantime I think the suggestion is a wise one, that we wait until we receive the report of the Civil Service Commission before taking any action. The bonus might be retained temporarily until something definite can be done, but I agree with the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil), that those who are in the service of the country should not assume the role of dictating to parliament, for after all we as the representatives of the people are, I am sure, anxious to do what is fair by every one.

subtopic: MOTION, MR. CHURCH, TO DISCUSS A MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE
speechtext:
I do not wish, sir to prolong this debate, however I deem it my duty to request the government to kindly keep up the civil service bonus, which was granted during the war at a time when the high cost of living prevailed, until reclassification of salaries takes place,
not only as regards the Post Office Department, but all departments as well. One should bear in mind that the cost of living has not gone down in proportion to the general wish of lowering the salaries. To-day, for instance, rents are 50 per cent higher than they were at the beginning of the war. The same is true for fuel and at present we are paying $16 per ton for coal. Indeed, I do not think thar the civil employees without the bonus can manage to live on the pre-war salaries.
I find it strange that it is always the salaries of government officials that we first pounce upon when it is a question of economizing. I think there are measures of economy that would be more equitable and more profitable to the country than the cutting down of the civil servants salaries. If there be too many employees, we may dispense with some; but let those who are needed and do the work receive a fair salary so as to allow them to bring up a family in a decent way and hold in society the rank which their position entitles them to. Again,
I did not wish to let this occasion slip by without protesting-not only on behalf of the electors whom I represent, but on behalf of the electors of the whole country-against the lowering of salaries, especially before a final report is brought down in the House. I entirely agree with suggestion of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. McGiverin) to continue the bonus to employees until the reclassification of salaries takes place for all departments.
Right- Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN( Leader of the Opposition): It is a mere platitude to say that like every other hon. member of this House I believe in fair salaries. The question as to what fair salaries are does not enter sharply into this debate, it does not enter now into the consideration of what the duty of parliament and of the government is in the premises. But, speaking of fair salaries, let me make this intimation to the government:	I think that the facility with which
they have yielded to the demand of the higher officials of the country for larger salaries year after year has had very considerably to do with increasing the unrest among those who are more moderately paid. The government, in so far as salaries have been within their own supervision and decision, have almost in every case yielded to pressure; and such salaries have now reached a scale very perceptibly above where similar salaries were at a time when the cost of living was virtually where it is to-day. This accentuates a situation which causes unrest and invites disturbance.
Postal Employees

I have always supported the principle of having the general scale of salaries investigated by an impartial tribunal and by that tribunal determined, and after its decision and recommendation to the government, placing upon the latter the responsibility of acceptance or rejection. This was the system established some seven or eight years ago; it is the system in force to-day. Under that system the government has a power of review, and if it is desired that the general scale recommended by the Civil Service Commission should be increased or diminished, any government knows that if it takes responsibility in the matter the commission will follow its suggestion. In the -time when the responsibility was ours, when we once accepted the commission's recommendation we stood by that recommendation, we took the responsibility for it and presented a united front to the service and to the country. Now, I say to the administration, I do not know whether there is to be a strike or not, but if ever a government invited a strike this government has done so by its vacillation, its pusillanimity, by- its determination to avoid every responsibility and not even to stand by the officials of the country. The government's course from the beginning has been an effort to incite the service against the commission; never has the Prime Minister risen that there has not fallen from his lips a reflection oblique or direct on the system and on the commission, an effort to show that the government's goodwill knows no bounds but that the commission sits over there holding fast the government's beneficent hands. If only the matter were in the power of the government, if the late administration and the late parliament had not tied its hands, how bountiful it would be; but the commission is in control, responsible government is gone, and this commission-ridden government is compelled now to submit to a restraint that it deplores! Has not this been the continuous attitude of the administration? Would anybody expect contentment in the service, or a belief that after every possible consideration had been given to their claims they had to abide by the decision or leave the service? All the service have been led now to understand that the usurper to be dethroned is the Civil Service Commission, that already it is looked at askance by the government, and that, if only they raise enough disturbance, down will go the despot and their liberty will be complete.
What is the history of this matter? We had first of all the Civil Service Commission. This commission pursuant to the duties imposed

on it by this House, some years ago recommended a classification and a scale of salaries in accordance therewith. The scale they recommended was designed for what they termed normal times, and they arrived at it by taking the ascending line of cost of living and of salaries which prevailed before the war, and projecting that line through the years of the war and the years thereafter right up to the time of the fixing of the scale; that is to say, they assumed that but for the abnormal conditions of the war the cost of living would have gone up at the same rate during the period of the war as it went up before, and they fixed the salaries accordingly. But they said to the government: We are quite aware that these salaries do not take account of abnormal living costs due to the war; these should be taken account of temporarily, because they are likely to be in themselves temporary; that responsibility of fixing a bonus was ours, and we fixed it as we felt right to meet the situation then prevailing. These are the circumstances that continued up to the period of this administration. There was some cutting of the bonus a year ago. At my hands this received no criticism. This year the government, anxious to make a display of economy, announced early in the session, or before, a very considerable bonus cut applicable throughout the service iSuch announcement was equivalent to stating that in the view of the government under the cost of living conditions of to-day the entire bonus with the salary fixed by the commission amounted to too high a total. When this decision was announced there was a protest on the part of the Civil Service. The government, afraid to stand to its guns, saw the commission sitting over there, and said: We will put it on them, if we can. And the administration made a reference to the commission and asked for a revision of the whole salary list again. This was the first attempt to avoid taking any responsibility, or rather to avoid continuing the responsibility which it had taken, because when it made the reduction it declared to the service that it believed what they were receiving was too high. When the protest became loud enough the reference followed. I have gone through sufficient of the return just brought down-I have not had time to go through the whole of it-to make clear to me that the words of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) were abundantly justified when he said in effect that if ever a commission or a body of men conscientiously went about its duties, this commission did. He states they received a representation from the post office employees

Postal Employees
once, and again a second time. This is true. But according to this return they received a representation a third time, and still a fourth time, before the final submission of their recommendation took place. And as far as the return shows, nothing in the way of information or opportunity was denied, save a demand that the actual figures of the commission's recommendation, which already had been before the government but not approved, should be made known. The justice of this refusal, of course, every hon. member sees. The duty of the commission was not to make public its recommendation until the government had approved it; the government would have justly found fault had the commission done so in the meantime.
Now I come to inquire as to just what is the result of the investigation and report. I am astonished that the government has not disclosed to the House the real situation-the real schedule as approved by the administration, indeed, I am astonished that it has not gone further, that it has not made known to the country the outstanding facts so that all could judge the merits of the situation, because on the general judgment of the country the ultimate solution depends. On the contrary, the government has risen, chiefly through the Prime Minister, to profess itself impotent, sorry that it is so, of course, and, to the applause of those behind it who crave for patronage, to declare, "The commission is there, and until it is got rid of or shorn of its powers the government can do nothing." Would not the government have been better employed if it had first ascertained to the best of its knowledge whether the commission had fully done its duty, taken all things into account, and then, having so decided and approved the commission's finding, had stood up in this House and said: "The commission is right and we are behind the commission, and we intend to stand behind it through all eventualities?" I think this would have been worthy the dignity of the country, and would probably have led to much better results than confront the administration now.
I am going to give the facts so far as I have got them from this return. The cost to the country in 1924-5, under the scale obtaining the year before with the bonus of the year before, would be 113,134,000. Consequently had the government not acted and made by order in council a reduction in the bonus, the cost to Canada this year would have been- estimated, of course, but doubtless very accurately-$13,134,000. This is the amount the government considered too large and determined to reduce. They made a reduction on
their own responsiblity, the total reduction being such amount as brought it down to $12,664,000; the difference, hon. gentlemen can calculate. Now, this is the reduction the government made. A protest then arose and the Civil Service Commission's work came in. The commission made a report, which was referred back but which subsequently was adhered to and constitutes the report approved to-day. On the commission's report the cost this year would be $12,956,000.

speechtext:
No. I rather think it is in the return, but I did not note it for the purpose of discussion. Now, I have gone far enough to show just what the effect of the finding is, and also just what the position of the government is. Let me add that when the commission made its recommendation first, the protest still continued. The government made a reference back and asked the commission to reopen the subject, stating the grounds to be as follows:
The Acting Postmaster General and the chief officials of his department feel that further occasion should
Postal Employees

be afforded them to make representations regarding certain anomalies apparent to them in the schedules submitted.
The fepresentatives of the employees have also requested that a wider opportunity be given them to present their claims and to discuss proposals than was found possible to be allowed them when they were heard by the commission in the matter.
That is to say, the government referred these schedules back because of anomalies claimed to exist by officials of the Post Office Department, and secondly, because the employees desired further opportunity to be heard. It will be noted that the government made no statement or comment whatever as to whether the general scale and total were too high or too low. Having the reference back, the commission again heard the employees, once or twice,, I am not sure which. They heard the post office officials, and the post office officials made recom-S p.m. mendations as to their own employees which, if they had been accepted by the commission, would have raised the total to $13,487,020. That is to say, the Civil Service Commission was faced with this situation: A salary scale of $13,134,000 reduced by the government.to $12,664,000; and at the same time the government's own officials of the Post Office Department coming to the commission and demanding a scale which would have totalled $13,487,020. In other words the commission was faced with a demand from the department for an increase of three hundred thousand odd dollars over the same figure which the entire government had reduced by $170,000. Hon. gentlemen will understand what part the government was playing in relation to the commission'-just the measure and quality of cooperation which was being afforded.
It is very natural for the officials of a department to seek a considerable scale for their own employees. I do not think there is a department of this government the officials of which will not argue-and probably argue conscientiously; certainly argue vociferously-that their employees are all paid too low compared with the employees of any other department. Naturally the post office officials so contend, and they put before the commission a scale which would have put the total at over $354,000 above the total from which the government had reduced it in order to make a display of economy to the people of Canada.
The employees, on the other hand, made their representations, as they had a perfect right to do.

I venture to say that
taking into consideration all the changes in working hours the post office officials had in mind, the amount involved would still aggregate a figure substantially above the total which existed before the government's reduction. The emplojmes presented claims which in the estimation of the commission would have involved a payment this year of $15,055,000. Such was the plight of the commission. They placed before the government the major considerations which they felt should guide them in the discharge of their duty-recited them one by one; and I venture to ask hon. members to read the report of the commission and to read the recital of those factors which governed the commission in their decision. If hon. members do, they will say that regard was paid to those very things to which regard ought to be paid in coming to a conclusion in a matter of this kind.
It is surely the duty of hon. members of this House to be fair to the Civil Service Commission. If there is a body of men that has a difficult, well nigh impossible, task in this country it is that commission. They have to stand between the taxpayers of Canada and those who have to gain by importunities at their door; and they apparently also have to stand between the desire of the taxpayer for economy and the desire of the government for evasion and popularity as the prize of evasion. This seems to be the position that the commission is in. Now, on the last report being forwarded a confirmation of the first, with all the reasons, it was almost an intimation as to what the cost to Canada would be if the higher scale were followed -either the higher scale of the post office officials' recommendations or of the postal employees-what the whole cost to Canada would be applied over the entire service, and this information is in the hands of the gov-

eminent now. In the presence of these facts the government approves and that scale becomes the law of the land.
When a strike is threatened what is the conduct of the' administration? Yesterday when the matter was called to the attention of the Prime Minister he rose and delivered himself of these words-I invite the attention of the House and the country to them as illustrating the position this government assumes in the face of what now confronts this Dominion:
Parliament also gave to the commission like powers-
Having referred before to its powers as to appointments.
-with respect to revision of salaries of civil servants, so that the power of revision of salaries of civil servants is taken away entirely from the government. This illustrates wherein to some extent we are being governed by commission and not in acordance with a system of a responsible government in the strict meaning of the term.
If this is not an attack upon the commission, on the whole system, I should like hon. members to define to me what is. Here is a declaration to the Dominion that the Civil Service law at the present time constitutes government by commission and is a negation of responsible government. Could a plainer incitement be thrown out to all those who feel they are not getting what they want at the hands of the commission an incitement to go on with the attack and the onslaught because the very institution they are attacking has not the support of the government itself? Then he goes on:
The government, appreciating the position, took care at the outset to associate with the conmission in the matter of revision of salaries of civil servants, in particular the salaries of postal employees, which were the first to be referred to the deputy ministers and the Board of Audit. On each of two occasions that a report was made by the commission, having learned that the report was not acceptable to the postal employees, the government took such steps as were possible to secure a further consideration by the Civil Service Commission of their report. The government has gone in that direction just as far as it is possible to go in the matter, and as my hon. friend has said, if there is to be any further change in salaries, they will have to be made by parliament itself. The government is placed in the position, either of asserting that it is not prepared to accept the legislation which is on the statutes and of being obliged jn consequence to ask parliament to enable it to revise or amend that legislation, or to stand by the legislation as it appears. We have not felt, at the present, at least, that we would be justified in asking parliament to amend or repeal the statute under which the Civil Service Commissioners have acted, nor to take action in any way other than in accordance with the recommendations of the commission.
What is the whole tenor and purport of that statement yesterday? Does it embody the slightest intimation that the government
Postal Employees
stands by the commission in the prosecution of its work? The slightest intimation that the government is prepared, in the event of a violation of the responsibilities of parliament and of this House, to stand by the recognized authorities of the country? Why, it is an intimation in every line that the government is not satisfied with the situation, it is an intimation to all those who threatened trouble that there is ground for their complaint, and the reason the ground exists is because parliament has tied the hands of this benevolent government and if it had not done so all these grievances would have been redressed. I want to know from the Minister of the Interior, in whose speech to-day I found a little more inspiration than in that of any other member of the government on this subject, whether he thinks that quotation reflects a manly stand, whether he thinks it reflects a stand worthy of the dignity of this House?

This is the fine fortitude displayed by the government this afternoon. I do make this appeal. There is fairness coming to everybody. I made a note of my
hon. friend hedging and dancing round that point when he referred to the duty of the government, and what a pusillanimous government it was and that when the report came back it could not do one thing or the other. The Department of Justice has stated that all the government can do under the act is either to reject or approve. Would my hon. friend say we were right if we had rejected the report? Of course he would have said we were wrong no matter what we did, but would the country have said we were right had we rejected the report? What would have happened if we had rejected it? There would have been chaos, or another report would have been brought in which would have been exactly the same, and then another rejection. That was not the government's idea. The government saw that there was a vast difference of opinion between the postal employees and the Civil Service Commission on the one hand and, the postal department and the Audit Board on the other. I agree with the right hon. gentleman that when the Civil Service Commission made its report it gave good and substantial reasons for their finding. The matter was then referred to the Audit Board, who, except in some of the higher classes, I think, practically agreed with the finding of the Civil Service Commission. In order-and I appeal to hon. members on both sides of the House on this point-if possible to get unanimity of opinion expressed in their report, the Audit Board and the Civil Service Commission were brought together to discus before the government-not alone but to discuss in the presence of the government in the council chamber-their differences and their reasons. Now would it not have been a good thing if the Audit Board and the Civil Service Commission could have been brought together and made a report to which they both agreed? Certainly it would. That is what the government did. After the Civil Service Commission had heard all the Audit Board had to say in reference to its stand, its members took all these things into consideration; and were asked by the government, in view of all these things and the new light that might have been brought to them, if they desired to make any change in their report. They took a few days to consider, and made no change in the report. I want to say distinctly and not offensively that the government is standing by the Civil Service Commission because it is the body authorized by statute to make this report and to give a decision. There has not been any abuse of the Civil Service Commission, because the government did its best, on behalf of the peace and good government of Canada, on behalf of the employees of the govern-
Postal Employees

ment and of the commission itself, to ascertain if it were not possible to have unanimity in the finding or in the conclusions of the Audit Board and of the Civil Service Commission. That unanimity was not arrived at, and under the statute the government has approved of the action of the Civil Service Commission.
Referring to the strike, I am sure I will not say anything to incite a strike. I am inclined to think that some things have been said here to-day that will not mollify the feelings of the gentlemen who are inclined to striks, but will furnish encouragement for them to do so. I say now to the postal employees of the Dominion of Canada that the men who advise them not to strike are their friends far and away beyond those who advise them to strike. The parliament of Canada is always in >a position to deal with situations if it is allowed to do so, but employees can put themselves in a place where parliament can only do one thing, and that is not what the postal workers desire. My right hon. friend, of course, abused the government. I am not surprised at that. That is a habit. As Harry Lauder would say, "That is nae a habit, it's a gift".
One of the reasons my hon. friend ascribed for this unrest in the Civil Service was the fact that some of the officials in the higher grades had their salaries increased. I want to say right here, with some experience, that the majority of the men and women in the Civil Service who get the higher salaries can obtain better salaries in other walks of life. Men and women who are taking the full responsibility for the expenditure of millions of money, handling work of great importance in this country, can almost at any time they desire have their salaries increased by going to a private concern. That happens time after time, and the reason why salaries were raised -and it was a selfish reason in many cases- was in order to retain the services of men who would otherwise leave the service and secure higher salaries. I can instance man after man in the higher salaried positions of the Civil Service at Ottawa who can, in ten days, secure a better position than he has now at Ottawa. The worry and the responsibility of one of these men in the higher positions of the Civil Service of Canada, to say nothing of the work is sufficient to drive the best men out of the service, and I am surprised sometimes that we are able to keep them. I believe it is only on account of their devotion to public duty that we are able to retain some of the men in the higher positions of the service of this country.

One of the difficulties in the Civil Service- my right hon. friend referred to it from another angle-is the fact that everybody in the Civil Service knows what every other person in the service is receiving. Publicity in that respect, many members of parliament will say, ri good. But knowing what it is to be at the head of a department, let me say that the jealousies arising in the Civil Service create a great unrest, and if one of the clerks comes with a complaint, it is not that he or she is not well paid, but that another employee beside him or her is not doing any more w'ork, but is getting better pay. If we could devise some means by which, no person in a department would know what salaries the other employees are receiving, that would remove a great deal of the jealousies in the Civil Service.
I do not know what else the government can do. The government is behind the Civil Service Commission in its report. The threatened strike is undoubtedly a serious matter; but I say now-and I want to say this without any harshness-if, under all the conditions at present existing, the postal employees are not prepared to await the final decision of the Civil Service Commission for all the service, but inisist on putting the business of this country into a great turmoil, then the parliament of Canada is not responsible for that, but they will have to take the responsibility. I appeal to them, to their friends to advise them not to take that responsibility, but to accept what has been done in the legal, constituted way through the Civil Service Commission, and perform their duties under the new schedule, because there is not so much difference between it and their demands and the old schedule. I would suggest that they wait until the decision of the Civil Service Commission has been arrived at for all the service, and parliament may then decide in its *wisdom, not to over-ride the Civil Service Commission, but to devise some method by which an adjustment can be made that may be nearer the desires of the postal employees.
What I want to make clear is that the government has done its duty to the employees of the postal department; it has done its duty to the parliament of Canada, and it is prepared to accept all the responsibility for what has been done. We do hope and trust that the postal employees will not be misled into taking an action which will make it more difficult for parliament to deal with the matter in a manner that it might otherwise desire to do.

speechtext:
,Mr. Speaker; I am very glad that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) has brought before parliament this matter of the dissatisfaction of the postal employees with this proposed salary revision. I had intended in response to urgent messages which were sent to me from the postal employees of the city of Calgary, to bring this matter up to-morrow in a similar way, in which case I would have required some data with respect to the cost of living and salaries, which I had not. I am glad, however, that the matter has been brought up and that so many hon. members have expressed their opinions. I am delighted to know that no hon. member so far has even hinted that the dissatisfaction of the postal employees is in any way unfounded, although at the same time a number of hon. gentlemen have kept as far away from the real problem as, I think, they could possibly get. Theoretically, the Canadian parliament is supposed to be supreme in all matters, and surely a question that involves the possibility of a strike of public servants is well within the jurisdiction of a parliament that claims to be supreme. At the same time it appears to me that ministers of the Crown have become involved in some way by placing the Civil Service Act and the Civil Service Commission between this parliament and the proposed strikers outside and saying virtually this: Now, if you are going to strike, just look at this; here is the Civil Service Act. That is all we can say to these men. We are virtually declaiming against our own boasted theoretic power. I do not propose even to suggest that the Civil Service Act or the Civil Service Commission shall come between me and my duty or parliament and its duty with respect to the matter which has been brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for North Toronto.
The question really is not one of the Civil Service Commission, although much of the debate between members of the government and of the opposition has circled around the Civil Service Commission. The real question is: Are the proposed salaries of the postal workers sufficiently high to keep them from striking? The employees have not said: We are going to strike because you have a Civil Service Commission. They have said: We are going to strike because the proposed salary revision is too low. We have not heard very much comment on the part of the government with respect to that question, and that is the question. I could not hear the hon. member for North Toronto when he was speaking. I presume, however, that he reviewed briefly 209
the history of the negotiations of the employees in regard to salary revision.
Hon. members know that a cost of living bonus was added to the salaries of civil servants involved in order to meet the increase in the cost of living caused by the war. That has gone on until the present year when the government has proposed to remove it. Last year they removed part of it. This year they proposed to remove it all. They, however, suggested that the bonus would not be removed; that it would be added to the salary. It is very well understood, I think, that the postal employees looked upon the salary plus the bonus as being too low, and they had looked forward to the proposed revision in the hope that their salaries would be increased. But when the proposal came from the Civil Service Commission, it was discovered that there was a substantial reduction from what they received last year. It is not more than six weeks, I imagine, since the postal employees threatened to strike last time and as a result of that threat there were renewed negotiations. The schedule was sent back to the Civil Service Commission for revision; the final revision has come up, and again the postal employees have made clear their dissatisfaction with this proposal and threatened a strike in consequence.
I was rather amused to hear the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) a moment ago suggesting that the postal employees should wait until the complete report of the commission comes down; that is to say, they should wait until they know what some other class of civil servants are to get before they go on strike. So far as I can see, that is very poor advice. What difference would it make to the postal employees if the report should give twice as much in the way of salaries to some other class, or half as much, or put them on a similar basis? What difference in the world would that make? Would it put any more money into the pockets of the present employees of the postal department? I think not; yet it would have to convey a promise to do something of the kind before it could be considered good advice to the men who have threatened to strike, or induce them to stay their hand.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil), who I understand is acting as Postmaster General, suggests that this is not the logical way of meeting the situation; I presume he means that to bring the matter of the revision of salaries of the postal employees to the attention of parliament, as is being done now, is not the proper mode of procedure. He goes on to indicate to us

Postal Employees

liow the Civil Service Commission arrived at its conclusions, and he points out to us that this body is the logical one to deal with salary revisions, that it is impartial, that its actions were approved of by the Audit Board, and so forth. This of course is all very interesting and it is perfectly all right. But the point is that it has not been approved of by the people whom it most concerns, the people who will receive the salaries which have been fixed by the commission. The minister did not tell us whether the employees concerned had been consulted when the revision was made. What I want to know is upon what basis this competent body arrived at the present scale of salaries for the postal employees.

speechtext:
I understand that the postal workers did present their claims; but to present claims and to be consulted in regard to the revision of salaries are, from my point of view, two entirely different things. Indeed, the postal employees are presenting their claims in the present instance, but that does not constitute any sort of consultation. Now, the situation is approaching an industrial warfare, and I do not see that there is much difference between the presentation of the claims of the postal employees to the Civil Service Commission, to which the minister has just referred, and the present manner of presenting those claims, except that at the present time there is a threatened strike. The matter is a little more decisive in its present character than was the mere presentation which the minister has interpreted as a consultation.
I am speaking from memory, but I think that the average estimate made by several bodies in Canada of the minimum amount required for the maintenance of a family of five is approximately $2,000; that is about the average estimate for such a family. We find, under the salary revision of the Civil Service Commission as it applies to the postal employees, that many of these workers, in fact the large majority of -them, will have to work for half or less than half what is estimated as being necessary to maintain a proper standard of living for the average Canadian family. So -that it would1 be interesting to known upon what basis the Civil Service Commission arrived at the proposed salary list.

But I am more interested at the moment in what is going to be the attitude of parliament towards the threatened' strike. And this question was dealt with by both ministers of the Crown who have commented upon the subject before the House. The Acting Postmaster General wants to know whether we are merely to succumb as a parliament to the threat of the employees without an inquiry to ascertain whether there is any real difficulty under which these men are suffering. And he suggests that parliament should of all things be firm; in other words, parliament must actually resort finally to the club. The minister, I believe, declared that we must be fair and then be firm.
