I assure the House that I
had no intention of misquoting the words of the minister; I believe his exact words were that we should be fair and then firm. I know that there is probably no hon. member who is fairer than the Acting Postmaster General, and I do not think that there is anyone who is kinder than he is. I do not suggest for a moment that the minister himself wants to resort to the club; but I do say that he has left no otheT course open to parliament. Merely to express the opinion that parliament wants to be fair first and then to be firm is all very well. But when parliament has nothing fair to offer, when parliament completely abandons the course of fairness and simply has nothing left but the club, then the club is what parliament will use.
There are two methods which parliament might adopt in this matter:	One is the use
of intelligence and the other the use of the club. If intelligence is to be applied it means that we must meet the situation precisely as it exists at the moment; it does not mean that the leaders of the two great historic parties shall get into a scrap as to whether the commission should or should not be. The question is, are the wages that are being paid to the civil servants in question too low? If they are too low, then what are we going to do to increase them and thus to prevent the threatened strike? That is the question to which we must apply intelligence; and if we do not deal intelligently with the situation there is only one thing left for parliament and that will be the club, in the event of the employees in question carrying out their threat.

Postal Employees
I do not believe in strikes personally; I do not think they settle any question. But what I believe, or what any hon. member believes in regard to strikes makes no difference; strikes will occur if proper steps are not taken to ward them off. Under the existing situation they are inevitable. So that the question still confronts us, shall we apply the method of intelligence or shall we use the club? Upon the answer to that question will depend whether or not a strike occurs in the present instance. I want to point out that no hon. member has expressed the opinion, at least so far as I have been able to gather, that the salaries now paid postal employees are at all too high; no suggestion of that kind has been made. I think therefore I am justified in concluding that in the opinion of those who have spoken these salaries are if anything too low.

At six o'clock
I was referring to the manner in which this

government had used the Civil Service Commission in connection with the question under consideration. I had recollected nothing which gave the House the truth as to how the Civil Service Commission was seized of this dispute, and I invited my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to furnish me with the references, if there were any. I do not propose to go through them all. My right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) dealt with the last reference by the right hon. Prime Minister; I will give another just for the purpose of making absolutely clear what has happened in this case-that this House, yes, and the members of the Civil Service have been allowed to go on in the belief that the reference to the Civil Service Commission was for the purpose of increasing salaries, while as a matter of fact the reference was made necessary by the reduction of the bonus effected by the government. I turn to Hansard at page 3158 dealing with this question, and there I find the following statement by the Prime Minister on June 13 last:
The government, in order to ensure the fairest possible consideration for civil servants in that connection, required that the Civil Service Commission should prepare its report in conjunction with the deputy ministers, and also in conjunction with the Audit Board.
The government has taken particular care to see that the commission should carry out its wishes in that regard, and has on two or three different occasions referred back the report submitted by the commission to the government, before its final acceptance. I may mention that on the first or second occasion on which the Civil Service Commission submitted its report the report was signed by two of the commissioners. The postal employees requested that if possible the government obtain the signature of all three commissioners before accepting any report from them. The government insisted on that additional step, and the position of matters now is that the report has been made. The government had either to approve it or disapprove it. To disapprove it was to leave the salaries where they were; to approve it was to give effect to such increases as had been made by the Civil Service Commission.
Let us get behind the smoke screen and see what the real truth is. The salaries now paid, including the bonus, amount to $13,134,000. Then the government's proposal came along for reducing the bonus, resulting in the entire bill for salaries and bonus being cut down to $12,664,000. It was as a result of this proposed cut in the bonus that the question was referred to the Civil Service Commission, and the commission in its report fixes the whole amount at $12,956,000. Now, what is the government's quarrel with the commission? If the government be-by accident-consistent for a short period of time, its quarrel must be, not that the commission has cut too much, but that it has not cut enough off the

Postal Employees
bonus. The government's cut was $470,000; the cut made by the Civil Service Commission is $178,000.
Now, the point made by my right hon. leader absolutely stands,-that this government has in every possible way invited trouble and taken the position all along, so far as the public and this House are concerned, that the commission was the only obstacle which prevented the government being just-yes, being liberal with the postal service. That was their attitude, an attitude of finding fault with the commission instead of helping it. It is quite true that to-day the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) states boldly and definitely that the government stand behind the commission's report. Well, it is a great pity that the government did not try to do something to strengthen the hands of the commission if they were going to stand by its report; before they did everything they could to ruin its reputation and to make it easy for anything to be said against the report. I suppose it is still open to the government to make an eleventh hour repentance, but they have worked hardship in the meantime. Even the Globe to-day points out exactly what has been pointed out before, that if any real injustice is being done there is no trouble about remedying it, that it is idle to hide ourselves behind the skirts of the commission, that the real responsibility is on parliament. The Globe also points out some oases of apparent hardship. I do not know whether it would be a hardship or not on the government, but I do know that it was the direct duty of the government to go carefully into the whole matter and to see to it that justice was done. That in any action they may take in this very, very grave question which they have before them for decision they should carefully weigh the effect their action is going to have on public opinion throughout this whole Dominion. I may offer my opinion as an individual that if a strike takes place under the present circumstances public opinion throughout Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, will not support the postal workers in that action.
The law is on the statute book, and for the time being that law must stand. If I may offer a suggestion to the postal workers, it would be that they first ask that the law be changed. I think that is a very grave action for them to take. I am satisfied of this, Mr. Speaker- and I think I am within the judgment of the House when I make the statement-that every member of this House desires to do full justice to not only the postal employees of the Dominion but to every other civil servant in this country, both in regard to the question of salaries and the question of working conditions. A good deal has been said in the discussion this afternoon by my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) and his colleague from East Calgary (Mr. Irvine), and a reference was made to it by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), who has just spoken, as to the necessity of a decent wage or a living wage. I think my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg used the term "a decent standard of living." What is a decent standard of living? What is there that determines a decent standard of living? My hon. friend from West Calgary-and I have some regard for his ability and judgment-has quoted here tonight, American, Canadian and other authorities, as to what constitutes a standard of living, what constitutes a satisfactory wage. That depends altogether on the standard of living. If the parliament of Canada is to adopt a principle of fixing a wage in consonance with a certain standard of living, what is that standard of living to be? Are you going to measure it by the living conditions of the farmer out on the prairie or the farmer in the Maritime provinces or the fisherman down by the sea? I want to say in all seriousness to this House that there are in western Canada to-day tens of thousands of [Mr. Crerar.l
farmers who work hard the whole year round and who do not have but a fraction of what is said here to-night to be a living wage.

Canada.

Under the salaries existing at the present time or that have existed during the past year with the bonus that has obtained in the past year, the total amount drawn by the postal employees of Canada was $13,134,000. Under this schedule as laid down by the Civil Service Commission, they propose to reduce this to $12,956,000, or a difference for all the postal employees of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific of $178,000. If we study the statistics, the index figure of the Department of Labour or of the Bureau of Statistics, you will find that the line is coming steadily downwards in the cost of living. Only this morning I noticed in one of the morning papers published in this city a comparison of wholesale prices for May of the present year with May of 1920, when we had the peak of prices in this country as well as throughout the rest of the world. I wish to support a suggestion that was made first this afternoon by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). The Civil Service Commission are at present engaged in a revision of those salaries. At the request of the government, they tackled first the salaries of the postal employees and to-day they are engaged in an inquiry into salaries prevailing in other departments. I think there is some force to the point urged by the hon. member for North Waterloo that there should have been no disturbance of salaries and bonus until the whole classification of salaries had been made so that the whole thing might be done at once.
No one deprecates more than I the difficulties and disastrous consequences that may flow from a strike of the postal workers in this country. I am not going to discuss at the present moment the question whether postal workers or government employees of any kind have a right to strike under any conditions. I have my views on that question, and possibly at a future time in this House I may have an opportunity of expressing them. That question, however, is not germane to the discussion at the present moment. It is of the greatest importance that a strike at the present time should be averted if that possibly can ibe done. I appreciate the fact that the postal workers, in the position they have taken, have gone so far that it may be difficult for them to recede, and under those circumstances, there is no loss of dignity to the government or to the parliament of Canada if the position is frankly taken: Well, we do not admit your contention; but we think that this salary schedule should not have been put into effect until the whole matter of salary revision had been considered by the Civil Service Commission in its relation to all departments;
consequently we put you back upon that basis until we have the full report from the Civil Service Commission, and then we shall decide.

I
trust that as a result of the discussion which we have had to-day the parties will get together and this matter will be settled satisfactorily. Parliament is supreme in this country, and neither parliament nor the government should seek to evade herein the responsibility which properly belongs to it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon rather intimated that the present situation did not constitute an emergency, and I understand that the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) is of the same opinion. I do not by any means agree with these hon. gentlemen; I say most decidedly that there is an emergency. The present situation is a very serious one and the responsibility rests not upon the Civil Service Commission but upon the government to see that proper steps are taken, and taken without any delay, to have matters satisfactorily adjusted and a strike avoided. We are supposed to have representative government in this country, and as I have said, parliament is supreme in all these matters and can revise the decision of the Civil Service Commission or any other commission. There is therefore no reason whatever why the government should seek to shirk its legitimate responsibility. We have not made much progress in disposing of this vexed question in the past six months; it has been bandied about between one department or commission and another and has been passed on from deputy ministers and heads of government to the Civil Service Commission and to a new body known as the Board of Audit with no apparent results. No satisfactory settlement has been arrived at; the recent revision of the Civil Service Commission as presented to the men of the post office proves more unsatisfactory than ever. The scale of wages which has been proposed is utterly unsatisfactory and most unfair to the older employees, the sorters and letter carriers, and all those men who have grown old in the service.
It is all very well to say that if these men strike on service their places can be filled again. That is absolutely untrue; you cannot fill at a moment's notice the position which is held by any one of these older employees. Take for example such an emergency as occurs at Christmas; does any hon. gentleman contend for a moment that a merely temporary employee who has had no experience whatever could take the place of an old sorter or any other postal employee

Supply-Indian Affairs
who has spent a number of years in the service? It simply cannot be done; no one can learn the post office business in a day, whether it be in the position of a sorter or a letter carrier or in any other capacity. Furthermore, very grave responsibilities attach to those who have to deliver registered mail; the responsibilities on the rank and file are greater and altogether the work of the- postal employees, particularly of those men who have grown old in the service, is onerous and calls for the most satisfactory remuneration which the country can afford. The postal service has given every satisfaction, and moreover it is a public utility which is self-sustaining and gives service at cost including low labor costs.
In the city from which I come the revenue in this department amounts to $6,000,000 as against an expenditure of some $2,250,000. and a large profit is made from the Toronto post office. Now, the country is not bankrupt, nor is the Post Office Department in any impecunious state; so that there is no excuse for any evasion on the part of the government of its responsibility or for placing it on any commission. And if the government does seek to evade its responsibility in this matter I hope that the House at all events will do its duty. Let me read what the Deputy Minister of Justice, Mr. New-combe, has said in regard to the question of regulating the rates of compensation to be paid employees. These are his words:
The Governor in Council has, in my op inion, no authority to regulate rates of compensation independently. He may approve the rates submitted by the commission for approval, and the rates will thus become effective, but he has no authority to approve or sanction any rate in excess of that which is rceommended by the commission. Such an increase can be sanctioned only by parliamentary authority.
The government shelters itself behind all this and seeks to evade its responsibilty. The commission is subservient to parliament. In view of the fact that at six o'clock to-night, it was announced, the voting of the employees on the question as to whether or not there should be a strike throughout Canada closed it seems to me that the government must realize the extreme gravity of the situation; there can be no doubt whatever as to the existence of an emergency in this case. Tomorrow evening as I understand, unless the matter is satisfactorily settled, there is likely to be an interruption in the service. The president of the Board of Trade of the city of Toronto after carefully considering this revised schedule, gave it as his opinion that there was just foundation for the claims of the men. The department by the new schedule and
after turning the bonus into straight salary shows a saving of some $179,000 all told, and there is no reason why the government should not meet the requests of the postal employees. Let me say in conclusion once again that upon the government and not upon the Civil Service Commission rests the responsibility of settling this problem; and if a strike occurs to-morrow night, paralyzing business that is already none too good and is suffering to a great extent, the blame will lie at the door of the government. Business conditions are bad enough as things are now and very little business in some retail lines has been done all spring on account of weather conditions and other unfavourable circumstances, so that the business of the country cannot afford to incur the loss that must result from a strike. The business men are demanding that this question be settled, and I am only fulfilling my duty as a representative of the Toronto district in bringing the matter to the attention of the House.

Mr, McQUARRIE:	The hon. member
for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), who is unavoidably out of the city to-day, asked me to mention the case of the Lake of the Woods Indians. I think a petition was forwarded to the minister signed by the chiefs and representatives of a number of tribes. Apparently there was some difficulty in connection with this petition. In the first place it was presented to the Indian agent at Kenora, who undertook to forward it to the department but who failed to do so. Later, I understand, Mr. James Robinson, of Kenora, who is very much interested in the

Supply-Indian Affairs
subject, forwarded the petition on to the minister, but- no acknowledgement was received until Mr. Robinson had communicated with the Prime Minister, and then after a further delay of two or three months an acknowledgement was received, from the deputy minister,
I think, stating that the matter would be looked into. The subject has been covered in a statement prepared by Mr. Robinson, which I think, has been forwarded to the department. The case is very concisely put in a foreword to that statement, and perhaps I may be permitted to read it. It says:
The Lake of the Woods Indians complain to the parliament of Canada of unfair treatment. They declare their treaty rights have been violated and gross injustice done -them for the past forty years. They charge that most of their agents have shown little interest in their welfare and are high-handed and domineering in their actions and do not recognize the authority of their chiefs.
A petition to the government containing statement of their grievances and asking for an independent investigation of their complaints was sent down on August 21st last and no reply was received until November 29th, and then only after complaint to the Prime Minister that no notice or reply had been received to the petition. Their solicitor writes a series of letters to the press setting forth their complaints, which are re-produced herein with a short summary of the situation. No action has been taken by the head of the Indian department in reply to their petition, and this statement is issued in the hope that the parliament of Canada will listen to their complaint.
At time of making of the treaty in 1873 no one had any idea of the value of their territory. In area it was a small province within itself, 55,000 square miles of some of the finest territory in Canada, rich in timber, minerals, fur and fish and much of it of splendid agricultural possibilities and now dotted with thrifty towns, villages, hamlets and farming communities.
They surrendered this territory after negotiating a solemn treaty with the government of Canada (treaty No. 3) and in return were allowed certain reserves, many of them containing valuable timber w'hich has been disposed of by their agents and the timber cut and removed. During past fifty years they have never had a statement of how much timber has been cut and removed or what dues have been collected or what amount of money is to their credit.
As to matter of schools, the Indian chiefs at the time of the making of the treaty made special requests in their talks with the commissioners asking that schools be established and that teachers be sent to instruct their young people with the knowledge of the whites. Within this agency there are 600 Indian children of school age without the advantage of education. The only schools within this agency are two, one at Kenora known as the Indian industrial school established by the Roman Catholic Church and another out at Shoal lake known as the Cecilia Jaffray School established by the Presbyterian Church. The area of their agency is equal to about 250 miles from east to west and 225 from north to south. The two schools mentioned are the only schools within their territory, neither of which was established under direction of the Indian department, but one of which, the Kenora School has recently been bought by the government but left in the care of the original owners.
Fifty years is surely long enough for the Indian department to have experimented on these people, yet after that length of time these Indians are in a 210
worse condition than when the government took away [DOT] their lands and made them "wards of the crown." When are they to become free men and made responsible citizens of Canada if education is denied them and they remain in a state of servitude?
Every honest self-respecting Canadian will blush and hang his head in shame when he reflects how these people have been treated by the government of Canada. Instead of being a happy and contented people they are gradually dying off and will ultimately become extinct. Is this the keeping of Canada's word of honour as expressed in the treaty referred to?
More than one of the provinces of Canada since entering confederation have asked for a re-consideration of their rights. Are not these people entitled to a review of their treaty rights and for further consideration at the hands of our government?
It is requested that an independent commission be appointed to consider
First the prayer of their petition and
Secondly to generally review and report on the best methods of making an honest effort to observe the treaty and bring their native citizens of Canada (indigenous to the country) to a state of civilization and advancement equal to their virility and self respect when in the primitive state as at the time of the treaty and give them some of the opportunities and advantages given to (in many cases) the questionable element of European immigrants brought into Canada, to enjoy the fulness and bounty thereof, at great expense and, in too many cases, to Canada's harm and hurt.	_

1.	Years ago our reserve contained a large number of peopfle, but through sickness and death, our numbers have been reduced to 14 families, about 70 people.

McKenzie, neglected and refused to give any statement as to the quantity of timber cut and removed by the Keewatin Lumber Co. on our Reserve 32B, on Black river, although requested by our Chief, Bob Roy many times, and that we have never received one dollar therefor.

We respectfully ask for investigation into these matters, that we consider our grievances.

Counsellor Sha-bah-tise. Counsel! or Peter White and twelve members of the Band.
It is pointed out in this pamphlet that in the United States the Indians have been very much better treated than have the Indians

in this country, at any rate, in the part of Canada referred to, and that as a consequence the former are now in a very flourishing condition; they are becoming educated and taking their places as citizens of the republic. It is also pointed out that in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan the Indians have been looked after and are now producing very large quantities of grain. I want to say that in repeating the foreword of this pamphlet and the petition of the Indians it must not be understood that I am making any charge. I notice in the pamphlet there is a reply from the Indian agent at Kenora to certain statements published in the Kenora press which explains various matters from the standpoint of the present agent. I am simply asking, on behalf of the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), that the case of these Indians be looked into, and that an independent commissioner be appointed to investigate the whole question.
I may say there seems to have been a good deal of controversy on these matters with the department, or at any rate with certain of the Indian agents who are now, or have been in the past, in the service. The main claim of the petitioners is in regard to the timber. It seems to me that the Indians are quite justified in asking for an accounting, and I do not understand why their request in that regard has not been granted. Apparently an accounting has been asked for many times. Surely they are entitled to know how much money their timber has brought, and how that money has been disposed of. If there is any sum to be placed to their credit they are entitled to know it. Apparently only one accounting was made by the department. Then there is the question of providing educational facilities. If these Indians are ever going to be lifted out of their position as wards of the government it seems to me they must be afforded some chance of obtaining an education. Apparently no facilities of this kind are provided for them at the present time. The Indians also want to be instructed in agriculture; they think they are entitled to the same treatment that has been extended to the Indians in Alberta and Saskatchewan. There is another demand to which they appear to attach considerable importance, namely, that some kind of a house of rest should be provided for them when they go to Kenora, as the Indians quite frequently do. They are not able to stay at hotels, because they would not be welcome guests, and there is absolutely no place in Kenora where they can put up. In conclusion I submit to the minister these requests should

receive consideration. These Indians have certain rights under the treaty and the government should be prepared to strictly carry out those rights.

We are inclined to smile here at the Indian situation in relation to the League of Nations, but at one time during the sessions of the assembly of the league it did not appear to be a laughing matter. The representatives of the Indians arrived at Geneva by way of London. They first made their appeal in London and went further to the League of Nations; through the Netherlands they made an attempt to become members of the league. While in Geneva the Canadian representatives, I would not say experienced difficulty, but at any rate were of the opinion that Canada might be placed in a false position before the league inasmuch as the Indian representatives with their legal adviser from across the line had stirred up considerable enthusiasm in their case in the city of Geneva. As the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) has pointed out the smaller nations seem to show great interest in the Indians' claim. They made the claim that they were neither British subjects nor Canadians; they declared that they were allies of Great Britain, their status having been recognized under an old treaty made many years ago. And when it was pointed out that they had served with the Canadian troops as Canadians overseas their reply was that they had done nothing of the kind but had gone overseas as allies of Great Britain, fighting side by side with other allies, who were Canadians. In short, they claimed the status o" a nation and asked to be admitted

to the ieague on that basis. There is an organization in Geneva for the protection of the Indians, and meetings were held nightly there protesting against the alleged treatment of these Indians by Canada. A deputation was sent from this association to wait upon the ex-Minisfer of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) and myself, asking why we had treated the Indians in such a manner. The Canadian delegation was at first inclined to be sceptical of the seriousness of the matter, but it soon appeared that the representatives of the Indians were really in earnest. In reply we directed them to send the Indians and their legal representative to us so that we might discuss the matter together. They never came, but at a meeting of the league the representatives from Persia were very insistent on a motion being made to have the whole question of the treatment of the Indians by the Dominion of Canada discussed in the Assembly. Application was made to Sir Eric Drummond, who I believe was secretary to the Assembly, and the matter was referred to the president and a certain board the name of which I cannot recall at the moment. It was decided that the Indians had no claim to a status in the league and their case wa?< not brought up in any way before the Assembly. For two or three days it seemed as though the Canadian representatives might be called upon in the Assembly of the League of Nations to defend the treatment of the Indians by the Dominion of Canada. When this attempt failed the representatives of the Indians remained in Geneva, and I am not sure that they are not there now. They remained there for a time disseminating propaganda, and I believe they wrent to Paris for a while and then on to London. The latest information I have is that at the next meeting of the Assembly of the League of Nations another attempt will be made by the Indians to be recognized as a nation in the League.

I am afraid I find my enthusiasm for the League of Nations actually waning. If it is spending its time on humbug of that sort it seems to me it might soon be time for us to consider whether we will vote the money Canada supplies.
That is what the Canadian representatives thought.
It will soon be as bad as the Canadian parliament.

I should like to point
this out: On the surface the amount paid in subsidies to steamship companies for these services looks like a lot of money, but it is possible there is just one feature that is not apparent to hon. members who have not lived in the small places served by these steamships. In many cases they are small communities on isolated islands or headlands and are without railway communication. Even with the existing service I think most of us would not want to be placed in the same position at all. Without these subsidies it would be impossible for them to have any
Supply-Steamship Services

regular means of communication. For example, take the case of a man who is raising produce in one of these isolated spots and wants to get that produce to the market in some of the larger towns. It is impossible for him to get across, we will say to Halifax, with his produce unless a regular service is provided. Without such a service there might be a danger of such places becoming depopulated. It is not only a matter of the inhabitants obtaining their mail but of getting their produce to market. And in many cases there would be great difficulty in inducing the shipowner to put his steamship on the route unless a subsidy wrere granted. I think I am safe in saying that without such a service there would be danger of these particular places becoming depopulated. The hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) would know more about the conditions because I imagine he lives very close to them. However, I know such a condition exists. I confess that it looks as though a lot of money is paid for these sendees but it provides a means of transportation to the people who are carrying on a line of production both in fishing and in farming, and it enables them to stay where they are and produce and maintain the population of the country. That being so I think it is money well spent.

I hope I did not leave a wrong impression on the mind of the hon. member. This applies to the people of the mainland because there are many communities so located. If you look at the map of the Maritime provinces you will find the coast line is very jagged; there are long points running out, and deep bays between the headlands. It is impossible to give people living in such places railway communication; in fact their only means of getting from where they live to market is by boat.

The hon. member talked
about islands.

I did refer to inlands
but communities on the mainland are similarly situated. The people on the mainland are perhaps not as isolated as regards transportation facilities as they are on the islands, but in many cases their only outlet is by the sea, the coast is a rough one and very broken, and very hard to navigate in stormy weather.

Even on the mainland the people may, in some cases, be eighteen to twenty miles distant from a railway. It is impossible to move these people from their homes; they would not want to go any more than we would wish to move ourselves. The only communication they have with the outside world is during the summer months, say from May until November. These little steamers run along the shore. I have no objection to
the policy of the minister regarding these mail subsidies and steamboat subventions, but I would like to find out from the minister the policy of the government, and on what principle these subventions are granted. No province in the Dominion is suffering to-day from the lack of transportation facilities as much as Ontario. Steamboat towns like Pic-ton and many other places are dead to-day, and the steamboat has been frozen out of the lake business in the province of Ontario owing to a monopoly. I would like to see the principle of the mail subsidy established in Ontario, and subsidies granted to the small steamboats. These boats have had to go out of business, for instance, on the bay of Quinte. They should be given a subsidy in return for services rendered, and we would have a better mail service. Dear knows, in rural Ontario the mail service is not what it should be, as has been explained by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys). I have no objection to these particular grants, but I doubt if they come within the meaning of the British North America Act as being works for the general advantage of Canada. I think the principle of granting subsidies should be extended to the province of Ontario and subsidies should be given to the boats running to towns on the north shore of lake Ontario and to boats calling at ports on lake Huron, where they have only one through service a day. Some of them have not even that. The result is that we have to depend very largely on the rural mail delivery. The Maritime provinces get this particular form of service from the Department of Trade and Commerce. I do not see why the principle should not be extended to the province of Ontario. Such subsidies have not been granted to this province.

In the province of Ontario
the service was started about twenty years ago from the mainland to Pelee island, and it has been continued ever since.
Mr. CHURCH. I am not objecting to the particular vote, because no doubt it is necessary, but every vote should be on a basic principle, and if you are going to adopt the principle of giving to the Maritime province services by boats and branch and trunk lines to rural places which have many other forms of transportation, the principle should be extended to Ontario. You are giving them a boat service and subsidizing that service. I brought up this question last year, and the
[Mr. Doucet.l
Minister of Trade and Commerce on that occasion appreciated my argument, as will be seen by a reference to Hansard. He said something was going to be done to give the boat service a chance in Ontario. It is time something was done in the way of subsidies and subventions to assist the boat business in Ontario. It is very badly needed. If you compare the mail service by boat on Georgian bay, and in the Muskoka district, and around Windsor on the Canadian side with the service rendered on the American side, you will see that we are far behind the times. If the Maritime provinces are to be given subsidies I think these subsidies should be extended to Ontario and other parts of Canada. They need some subventions to build up the steamboat business. It is not right to permit that business to be run by a monopoly. These boats cannot run without some assistance from the government. I am very much in doubt, however, whether these subsidies come within the British North America Act. However, if they come under the British North America Act, and the government is going to build up the Maritime provinces by granting these subsidies, the principle should be extended to Ontario. The rural parts of Ontario have been demanding better service. They have not the boat subventions and the mail subsidies which they should have and which the other provinces have. I should like to see the Maritime provinces get everything they can, because the country in my opinion did not keep faith with them. There are many parts of new Ontario and of old Ontario which have a very poor service and cannot under present conditions get a better service. The Canada Steamship Company has frozen out all these small steamboat operations at Sarnia, along the Detroit river and along the north shore of lake Ontario as far as Belleville. They have monopolized the boat business and driven all the small boats out of commission. The only remedy is to give the small boats a subvention. I hope the minister in the recess of parliament will look into the matter of subsidizing Ontario in regard to the boat business.
I object to the vote carrying. This Pelee island vote is the only one in the province of Ontario.

vote in?

There was no service last year. We are going to call for tenders.

Yes.

It looks as if there was not much business doing.

There cannot be a great deal
or somebody would take up this service. If any steamship company were sure that with the $6,000 subsidy a profitable service could be established the service would have been taken up.

Am I to understand that
these mail subsidies and steamship subventions apply only to the Maritime provinces? I cannot understand how, by the wildest stretch of imagination, these can be said to be works for the general advantage of Canada so as to come under the jurisdiction of this parliament. There are just as many ports in Ontario that have no form of transportation and that need a service for carrying mails and freight. In some of those places the mails and freight have to go by wagon route and other kinds of routes. That is the case in old Ontario, the Nipissing district, the Muskoka district, the district along the north shore of lake Ontario and many other parts of lake Ontario,
and the Georgian bay district. This principle should be extended to the province of Ontario. Just fancy what a difference it would make if a subsidy of $15,000 or $20,000 were given to a steamship company to carry mails and freight between Napanee and other places on the bay of Quinte and the county of Prince Edward. This county is stagnant today and the population has decreased on account of lack of transportation facilities. There used to be a boat service all along the bay of Quinte, but it has been frozen out today. If a subsidy could be given for a boat plying between Napanee, Desoronto and these other places, those parts of Ontario would come into their own, and they are just as much entitled to a mail subsidy for a boat to carry mails and freight as the Maritime provinces. I am not objecting to these mail subsidies and steamship subventions for the Maritime provinces, but there should be equality of treatment. Old and new Ontario alike are stagnant to-day and things are dead in that province simply because of lack of adequate transportation facilities. The minister should have a survey made of Ontario in order to see whether it would be advisable to grant subventions in order to build up the province and to act as a controller of rates. Three hundred and twenty-four municipalities in Ontario voted for a railway system of their own because they were so sick of the service that the steam railways were giving them, and a subvention of $10,000 a year for a mail and freight service would be enough to establish a boat service in all the small towns of Ontario along the Great lakes. This matter was brought up last year and the year before but nothing has been done. There is no province in the Dominion suffering worse than Ontario on account of lack of transportation facilities and I should be glad if the minister would make a survey of the province because the former minister was going to do so but did not take any action.
I shall be very glad to make a survey.

Are Mulgrave

It seems to be a very important place. Many of these services seem to radiate from Mulgrave or Port Mulgrave.
My friends from the Maritime provinces say that it is a very important place. Seriously though, it is the "jumping off" place between Nova Scotia and Cape Breton.

I might, perhaps, explain to
hon. members from other parts of the Dominion that Mulgrave is the connecting point between Nova Scotia and Cape Breton, and passengers from Halifax and other parts of the Maritime provinces get off at Mulgrave to take steamers for Arichat, Guysborough, Inverness, Cheticamp and other points along the shore.

Have we a breakwater or wharf at all these little peninsulas out in the sea? Are they little summer resorts for individuals?
Not at all. If my hon. friend would ask the Minister of Public Works, he would be glad to answer these questions.

Last year, when we were discussing the estimates of the Minister of Public Works we were building a dock for svery individual living around the shore there. Now we are providing a boat service for those people.

Item agreed to.
Port Mulgrave, St. Peter's, Irish Cove and Marble mountain, and other ports on the Bras d'Or Lakes, steam service between, $10,350.
Why the increase?

It is not possible for us to
carry on the service without this extra amount and the service is an important one. We are not losing money on it. Certain improvements are contemplated.
What are the proposed improvements?

I have not the details here but I shall be glad to show them to my hon. friend if he will drop into the office. The contract is only for one year and we can discontinue it next year if that is advisable.

The Bras d'Or lakes are of course inland waters; they are in the island of Cape Breton, and the service which is afforded under this vote accommodates a large farming country. The markets are in the mining centres of Cape Breton county and this boat is subsidized to perform a service which has been rendered now for twenity-five years. The service performed heretofore was not considered adequate. More ports of call have been added and in order to meet the requirements of the people who have no railway accommodation in that part of the country and who therefore are entirely dependent upon these subsidized steamers it is necessary that water communication shall be maintained. This service is an important one and is successful. As time advances and the population increases further accommodation becomes necessary periodically.
Is the population increasing?

In certain centres it is. Marble Mountain, and Iona are important farming districts, and the population has increased in these places and in the mining towns. There are more products consumed in the mining certres to-day and there is therefore a greater necessity for continuous communications.

Is the service
weekly?
It is a tri-weekly service.

I do not understand why there should be half a dozen different companies running boats on the Bras d'Or lakes. There are several places in the estimates where subsidies are provided for boats in these lakes. The Bras d'Or lakes are of course beautiful but they are not very large. Would it not be more economical if one concern had the whole thing in hand and if one subsidy were voted?

The same company owns all these different boats. For instance, the boat that operates in the north part of Cape Breton is owned by the same company that owns some other boat, such as the Richmond, which operates on a different route.
Item agreed to.

What will be the business to-morrow?

To-morrow we shall take up certain resolutions and bills standing in the name of the Minister of Justice. Following that probably we shall take up the bill in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce with reference to the Gold and Silver Marking Act, and probably one or two other bills. Thereafter we shall take the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, followed by the estimates of the Public Works department.

Will all the resolutions
standing in the name of the Minister of Justice be taken up, and if so are they first?

Among those that will be taken up will be Orders:	No. 22, second
reading of Bill No. 39 to amend the act to authorize re-arrangements and transfers of duties in the Public Service; No. 23, second reading of Bill No. 65, to amend the Judges
Act; No. 27, second reading of Bill No. 116, to amend the Exchequer Court Act; No. 28, second reading of Bill No, 117, to amend the Expropriation Act; and No. 32, second reading of Bill No. 120 to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act.
That ought to be enough.

The Minister of Justice
did not think that they would take very long, but it is just possible he may be under a misapprehension as to the length of time they will require. We shall also take Order No. 39, the second reading of Bill No. 176 to amend the Gold and Silver Marking Act, 1913. After that we shall go into supply taking up the estimates I have outlined. Before the House adjourns I want to say that by agreement, as I am informed, between the different parties interested the Church Union bill will be taken up on Tuesday next and the day will be devoted to the discussion of that measure. It is earnestly hoped by all those who are anxious to get through that hon. members will be on hand so that if possible the discussion may be concluded on that day.

The minister is quite right in so far as the leaders go; I agreed to Tuesday, but I had no opportunity to consult anyone else. If there is any hon. gentleman anywhere who has a very valid objection to the discussion taking place on Tuesday he should be allowed to express it now; the debate is an important one.

I understood that next Tuesday the question would come up with reference to the disallowance of the Alberta Tax Act. The Minister of Justice had agreed to have that question discussed then owing to the fact that it had been postponed for several days.

I spoke to the Minister
of Justice as to Tuesday being fixed for the discussion of the Church Union bill, and he was perfectly agreeable. It is a very important measure, and as it is thought wise that members should have notice several days ahead, I trust my hon. friend will not raise any objection to the course taken. The discussion of the other subject which he refens to can be transferred to another day without any loss of time.

Provided, then, that
this other discussion will take place some other day with the consent of the government, I have no objection at all.
